common_name: Silver Baby Agapanthus (Fragrant Dwarf White-and-Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Silver Baby is among the smallest agapanthus in general cultivation and is grown as much for its unusual fragrance as for its flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, with light afternoon shade acceptable in the hottest inland gardens. Silver Baby forms a tight, low mound of narrow evergreen foliage and sends up short scapes topped with rounded umbels of ice-white florets softly tipped in pale blue, the buds slightly ruffled before opening; unusually for agapanthus, the flowers carry a light, sweet scent that is easiest to notice at close range or in containers near a seating area. Its diminutive scale and long summer bloom window make it a natural choice for pots, raised beds, and tight edging where the larger species agapanthus would crowd the space. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the display tidy and encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps only occasionally, since like other agapanthus it flowers most heavily when its roots are a little crowded.

subcategory: spectacular large South African autumn bulb

planting.note: Plant large bulbs with the neck and upper shoulder exposed above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; this Western Cape fynbos endemic flowers on a bare scape in late summer to early autumn before its leaves emerge, so the planting site should stay dry and undisturbed through summer dormancy.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the shoulder exposed in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty soil in full sun, and withhold water through the summer dormancy that precedes flowering. From bare ground a stout, leafless flower stalk rises and opens into a dense, near-spherical umbel of 20-40 narrow, red to deep-pink, sunbird-pollinated flowers with recurved tips, forming a striking mophead display before a single leaf is visible. Once flowering finishes the whole seed head dries, snaps free of the stalk, and tumbles off across open ground in the wind, scattering seed as it rolls -- a dispersal trick shared with few other bulbs. Broad, strap-shaped leaves then emerge and persist through the cooler months, dying back again as the bulb heads into its next summer rest; expect several years from a young offset to first bloom, and avoid disturbing established clumps.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in lean, very well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Karoo lily is native to seasonally wet flats and depressions across the semi-arid interior of South Africa and tolerates long dry spells once established.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in lean, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun. In summer a rounded cluster of pink to rose, trumpet-shaped flowers pushes straight up out of bare ground on a short stalk, opening at or near ground level ahead of or alongside the foliage, and the blooms turn noticeably more fragrant after dark, when they draw night-flying moths as pollinators. Once flowering finishes, a broad fan of up to a dozen or more long, tongue-shaped leaves unfurls and spreads low across the ground through the rest of the growing season. This is a tough, drought-adapted bulb suited to a hot, sunny, lean spot such as a gravel garden or rock bed rather than average border conditions, and established clumps resent disturbance and are best left undivided for years at a time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; the thick grey-green leaves twist and spiral as they mature, and the bulb needs a distinctly dry rest through winter to bloom reliably.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, watering through the growing season but keeping the bulb nearly dry during its winter rest. Named for the coastal town of Knysna along its Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal native range, this Cyrtanthus is easy to recognize even out of bloom by its thick, greyish, strap-shaped leaves that twist into a loose spiral as they age. In late spring and summer, thick flower stalks carry a nodding cluster of 6-12 large, pendulous, tubular blooms that shade from fiery red or orange at the base to yellow and green toward the flared tips, a color gradient that draws sunbirds as pollinators in its native habitat. It is slower to reach flowering size than smaller Cyrtanthus species but rewards patience, and its sculptural leaves and bold flower color make it a favorite specimen for a sunny patio container where its dry-winter needs are easy to control.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed after the last spring frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the smoky green flower spikes are a distinctive foil for the more common white-flowered summer hyacinth.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 8-12 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Strap-shaped, blue-green leaves emerge first, followed in late summer by arching spikes of pendulous, bell-shaped flowers in an unusual chartreuse to smoky jade-green, carrying a sweet fragrance that is most noticeable in the evening. The muted green coloring reads as an accent rather than a bright focal flower, making it a useful bridge color toward the back of a mixed border or among grasses and other bulbs with bolder blooms. Culture matches other summer hyacinths: give it steady moisture through the growing season, let the soil dry somewhat once foliage yellows, and in climates colder than about zone 7, lift and store the bulbs indoors over winter.
